title: Peau d'Ane - Donkey Skin

full_text:
Once upon a time, there reigned a great and wealthy king whose stables housed the most extraordinary marvel in all the world: a marvelous donkey whose stall, instead of common straw and filth, was carpeted with velvet, for every morning, the beast dropped upon the flagstones pure gold coins, Spanish doubloons, and Portuguese crusados, supplying the kingdom with inexhaustible wealth.

The king lived in bliss with his beautiful queen, who bore him a daughter endowed with heavenly grace. But a sudden sickness struck the queen. On her deathbed, fearful that her grieving husband might fall prey to a cruel second wife, she made him swear a solemn oath: that he would never remarry unless he found a maiden whose beauty, virtue, and wisdom surpassed her own.

After years of mourning, the king sought a new queen, but none in the world matched the late queen's perfection—except his own grown daughter. Confused by grief and ill-counsel, the king conceived the unlawful desire to marry the princess.

Horrified by this unnatural suit, the virtuous princess fled to the secluded grotto of her fairy godmother, the Lilac Fairy. 'Fear not, my child,' the wise fairy advised. 'Do not oppose your father with harsh words, for that would provoke his wrath. Instead, demand impossible conditions. Ask him first for a dress the color of the clear weather and blue skies; until he provides it, you will not listen to his proposal.'

The king summoned his master tailors, threatening them with the gallows unless they succeeded. Working night and day, they created a gown woven of azure silk so luminous that it mirrored the purest summer morning.

The princess returned to the fairy in despair. 'Demand next a gown the color of the silver moon,' the Lilac Fairy instructed. The king's embroiderers worked by moonlight and brought a robe of woven silver that shone with heavenly radiance.

'Demand now a gown the color of the sun,' said the fairy. The king melted gold ingots into threads finer than gossamer and encrusted the fabric with diamonds, producing a dress so dazzling that mortals could scarcely look upon it without shielding their eyes.

Trembling, the princess returned to the grotto: 'What shall I do now, godmother? He has granted every wish!'

'Now,' smiled the fairy, 'demand the skin of his marvelous gold-bearing donkey. He will never consent to sacrifice the source of all his wealth.'

Yet the king's obsession was so blind that without hesitation, he ordered the donkey slaughtered and had its coarse, shaggy hide presented to his daughter.

'Now you must flee,' the Lilac Fairy commanded. She touched the princess's magnificent dresses, which shrank into a small walnut shell that could be hidden in a pocket. 'Smear your face with soot, wrap yourself in this foul donkey's skin, and run into the wilderness. No one will recognize you. Whenever you tap this ebony wand, your walnut shell and dresses will appear.'

The princess slipped from the palace under the cover of night. Wrapped in the crude hide, she wandered through distant provinces, begging for employment. Because she looked so wretched, villagers threw stones at her, calling her 'Donkeyskin.'

At last, she found employment as a scullery maid on a vast royal estate, cleaning the turkey coops, scrubbing the grease from iron kettles, and sleeping in a damp hovel behind the pigsties. Yet through all her degradation, her gentle heart remained pure and patient.

On Sundays, having finished her dirty labor, Donkeyskin would wash the grime from her face, lock her wooden door, and open her walnut shell. Dressing in her gown of clear skies, the silver moon, or the golden sun, she would admire her reflection and sing like an angel, finding solace in her secret grace.

One afternoon, the king's handsome son, who was hunting in the forest, wandered into the courtyard and peeked through the keyhole of the solitary hovel. He gasped in wonder: instead of the filthy scullery maid, he beheld a maiden of celestial beauty, dressed in a robe of sunbeams and diamonds!

Overcome with love, the prince returned to the palace and fell into a burning fever of longing. The royal physicians were helpless. When his weeping mother begged him to reveal his desire, he whispered: 'I desire a cake baked by the hands of Donkeyskin, and nothing else can heal me.'

Though disgusted by the idea of food prepared by the filthy drudge, the queen ordered Donkeyskin to bake a cake. The princess washed her hands in rosewater, sifted fine flour, added fresh cream and eggs, and kneaded the dough. As she worked, a tiny emerald ring of exquisite workmanship slipped from her finger and became concealed within the cake.

When the cake was baked to golden perfection, the prince devoured it eagerly. Biting into the crumb, his teeth struck the emerald ring. He concealed the jewel under his pillow and grew more passionately in love than ever.

The prince declared he would marry only the maiden whose finger fit the tiny ring. Trumpets sounded, and ladies of the court, noblewomen, and peasant girls flocked to the castle, but the ring was so slender that none could slip it past their knuckle.

'Have all the women in the realm tried the ring?' the prince demanded.

'All,' answered the chamberlain, 'except filthy Donkeyskin who cleans the turkey coops.'

'Bring her here!' ordered the prince.

The court laughed scornfully as the wretched figure in the foul donkey skin entered the marble hall. But when the prince held out the emerald ring, her slender, delicate finger slid into it effortlessly!

At that moment, the princess let the coarse donkey skin fall to the floor. The Lilac Fairy appeared, touching her with her wand, and revealed the princess clothed in her magnificent gown of sunbeams and diamonds, radiant as the dawn!

The king and queen embraced her with tears of admiration, and preparations were made for a royal wedding. Among the invited monarchs was the princess's father, whose mind had been cured of his madness by the fairy's counsel. Weeping tears of joy, he asked his daughter's forgiveness and bestowed upon her his entire kingdom, proving that true virtue may be eclipsed by sorrow, but like the morning sun, it rises in glorious triumph.
moral: True modesty and virtue may be concealed beneath the humblest disguise, but like pure gold, their radiance cannot be hidden.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
